journal_name: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and learning systems

abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a dynamical systems framework for understanding the expressiveness of deep neural networks, fundamentally reconceptualizing the relationship between network architecture and learning dynamics. We model neural networks as continuous-time dynamical systems where data propagation through layers corresponds to state evolution governed by nonlinear differential equations. The theoretical contribution establishes rigorous connections between architectural parameters—depth, width, skip connections—and topological properties of the resulting dynamical system, including attractor structure, basin geometry, and convergence rates. By applying tools from nonlinear dynamics and differential topology, we prove that networks with specific architectural patterns, particularly those exhibiting particular topological invariants, achieve superior approximation capabilities and generalization properties. This framework generates testable predictions about optimal network configurations for different learning tasks, providing a principled approach to neural architecture search grounded in dynamical systems theory rather than empirical evaluation alone. Furthermore, the analysis reveals fundamental relationships between neural network theory and computational neuroscience, demonstrating how biological neural circuit properties translate into design principles for artificial systems. Extensive experiments validate the theoretical predictions across diverse architectures including residual networks and transformer variants. This work establishes a new paradigm for understanding deep learning that transcends traditional complexity measures and provides mathematically rigorous foundations for neural architecture design.

This paper presents a significantly improved convergence analysis for training recurrent neural networks, addressing critical limitations in existing theoretical understanding. While prior work established convergence guarantees under restrictive assumptions such as diagonal dominance or symmetric weights, real-world RNNs frequently violate these conditions. We develop a novel analysis framework based on contractive mappings that provides meaningful stability guarantees for networks with general weight matrices and nonlinear activations. The key theoretical contribution proves that under mild spectral conditions—specifically约束 on the operator norm of the recurrent weight matrix—the hidden state dynamics become locally contractive, ensuring bounded gradient propagation across arbitrarily long sequences. This result substantially sharpens existing bounds on vanishing and exploding gradients by providing exact characterizations rather than asymptotic statements. We further extend the analysis to gated recurrent units and long short-term memory networks, demonstrating that the gating mechanisms naturally enforce contractivity conditions. The theoretical findings yield improved generalization bounds for sequence models, showing that RNNs satisfying contractivity criteria exhibit favorable algorithmic stability properties. Comprehensive experiments on language modeling and time-series forecasting validate the theoretical predictions, confirming that networks operating in the contractive regime achieve superior performance on long-term dependency tasks. This work provides practitioners with theoretically grounded design criteria and significantly advances our understanding of recurrent neural network optimization.

This paper introduces Oscillatory Neural Networks (ONNs), a novel neural architecture paradigm that fundamentally reimagines temporal computation through coupled neural oscillators. Unlike conventional deep learning systems that represent information through rate-based coding, ONNs encode patterns in the phase relationships between oscillating units, enabling fundamentally different computational mechanisms inspired by biological neural circuits observed in computational neuroscience research. The architecture employs networks of limit-cycle oscillators coupled through learnable synaptic connections, where information processing emerges from synchronization dynamics and phase-locking behaviors rather than traditional weighted summations. We develop a learning algorithm that combines spike-timing-dependent plasticity for unsupervised feature learning with a novel gradient-based optimization method for supervised tasks, creating a unified learning system that bridges biological plausibility with gradient descent training. The oscillatory dynamics provide natural handling of temporal dependencies without explicit memory mechanisms, while sparse spike-based communication enables exceptional energy efficiency. Extensive evaluations on temporal pattern recognition, speech processing, and sequence modeling demonstrate that ONNs achieve competitive accuracy with substantially reduced computational and energy requirements compared to conventional recurrent neural networks and transformer architectures. The learned phase patterns exhibit interpretable temporal structure, revealing how the network organizes information in time. This work establishes a new computational paradigm that leverages dynamical systems principles for building efficient, brain-inspired neural hardware.

This paper proposes Adaptive Sparse Coding Networks (ASCN), a significantly improved architecture for efficient inference in resource-constrained environments. While existing pruning methods achieve model compression through post-training weight elimination, they typically suffer from accuracy degradation and irregular network structure that limits hardware acceleration. ASCN addresses these limitations through a novel training methodology that simultaneously learns optimal weight values and sparsity patterns. The key innovation lies in a differentiable mask mechanism that dynamically allocates non-zero parameters across network layers based on their contribution to final prediction, guided by an evolutionary optimization procedure inspired by biological neural development. Unlike prior work that applies fixed sparsity ratios, our approach discovers task-dependent sparse structures that preserve critical representational capacity while eliminating redundant connections. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that learned sparse architectures achieve favorable generalization bounds compared to dense networks with equivalent parameter counts. The resulting networks exhibit structured sparsity patterns amenable to efficient implementation on neural hardware accelerators. Comprehensive experiments on image classification, object detection, and natural language understanding tasks show that ASCN consistently outperforms existing pruning and architecture search methods, achieving 10x parameter reduction with minimal accuracy loss. The approach generalizes across convolutional neural networks and transformer architectures, providing a practical framework for deploying deep learning on edge devices with tight computational budgets.
